title: Carbon budgets in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about carbon: how much we emit, how fast it is falling, and what the world has left to spend.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: The budget is the hard part.
paras: Emissions in Britain and Germany have fallen further than many people think, and the remaining global budget is smaller than many people think. Both surprised the room.
How to share what is left, between countries and between people, is where the real argument starts.

questions.q: Burning fossil fuels emits CO₂. On average, how much does each person in the world emit in a year?
questions.explain: The world average was about 4.7 tonnes of fossil CO₂ per person in 2024, and it has stayed just under five tonnes for over a decade. The range is enormous: the US emits about three times the average, India less than half. Methane, farming and land use add more on top.
questions.source: Global Carbon Project, Global Carbon Budget 2025 (via Statista and Our World in Data)

questions.q: Which sector produces the most greenhouse gases in the UK?
questions.explain: Domestic transport, mostly cars, vans and lorries, has been the UK's largest-emitting sector since 2014, at about 30% of the total in 2024. Emissions from power stations have fallen fastest as coal disappeared.
questions.source: DESNZ, 2024 final UK greenhouse gas emissions statistics; DfT, Transport and environment statistics 2024

questions.q: By 2025, how far below their 1990 level were Germany's greenhouse gas emissions?
questions.explain: Germany emitted about 649 million tonnes in 2025, 48% less than in 1990 but barely below 2024. Its legal target is a 65% cut by 2030 and climate neutrality by 2045.
questions.source: Umweltbundesamt (German Environment Agency), press release 08/2026, March 2026

questions.q: To keep warming to 1.5°C, researchers calculated an average 'lifestyle carbon footprint' each person would need by 2030. What was it?
questions.explain: The target was 2.5 tonnes per person by 2030, falling to 0.7 by 2050. Germany's greenhouse gas emissions alone already work out at more than 7 tonnes per person, and consumption footprints in rich countries are higher still.
questions.source: Hot or Cool Institute, 1.5-Degree Lifestyles, 2021 (targets restated in its 2025 update)

questions.q: Scientists estimated the CO₂ the world could still emit, from the start of 2025, for a 50% chance of keeping warming to 1.5°C. At today's rate, how long would that last?
questions.explain: The remaining budget was about 130 billion tonnes of CO₂, roughly three years of current emissions. Scientists now expect the 1.5°C limit to be passed, at least for a time.
questions.source: Forster et al., Indicators of Global Climate Change 2024, Earth System Science Data, June 2025

questions.q: Since 2021, Germany has charged a carbon price on fuel for heating and road transport. What was it per tonne of CO₂ in 2025?
questions.explain: The price was €55 a tonne in 2025, up from €25 when it began in 2021, and in 2026 it is sold within a range of €55 to €65.
questions.source: German Fuel Emissions Trading Act (BEHG); prices reported by Rödl & Partner and enter.de, 2025

questions.q: The EU is building a second carbon market for fuel used in buildings and road transport across all member states. When is it now due to start?
questions.explain: The new market was due to start in 2027. EU governments pushed for a one-year delay in November 2025; Parliament approved it in February 2026 and the Council gave final approval on 5 March 2026.
questions.source: Amended European Climate Law (2040 target), adopted March 2026; reported by Argus Media and ESG Today

questions.q: The UK's Climate Change Committee advised in 2025 how far UK emissions should fall below their 1990 level by 2040. What did it recommend?
questions.explain: The committee recommended an 87% cut by 2040, on the way to net zero in 2050. By 2024, UK emissions were already 53% below their 1990 level.
questions.source: Climate Change Committee, The Seventh Carbon Budget, February 2025
